title: Encryption edge cache failover and audit ledger playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for hardening private deployments with a focus on:
- safe DEK/KEK lifecycle during rolling upgrades
- deterministic failover of encrypted edge caches (prefix/cache stores) when KMS becomes unavailable
- an append-only audit ledger backed by an HSM-signed checkpoint for forensic readiness

Context and motivation:
We frequently get two types of customer constraints in private/VPC/on-prem installs:
1) intermittent connectivity between tenant application nodes and the central KMS (latency / network policy / transient maintenance).
2) regulatory requirement for tamper-evident audit logs that can be independently verified (e.g., financial audits).

This playbook describes a pattern that minimizes blast radius during KMS upgrades or outages while preserving the ability to audit key operations. It is intentionally modular so ops teams can adopt parts depending on their threat model and network topology.

High-level architecture summary (proposed):
- KMS layer: primary KMS (customer-managed HashiCorp Vault or cloud KMS) + optional HSM-backed root key (PKCS#11 interface) used only for signing/KEK unwrap operations.
- Edge cache layer: local encrypted caches colocated with inference nodes (Redis or LMDB) using envelope encryption (DEK encrypted with KEK).
- Fallback proxy: lightweight secrets-proxy at node that can provide cached DEKs and enforce TTLs when central KMS unreachable.
- Audit ledger: append-only log (WORM-like) stored locally and periodically checkpointed to a signed ledger entry using HSM private key.

Core design principles:
- Envelope encryption everywhere: DEKs (per-cache shard) encrypted with KEK; KEKs are short-lived wrapping keys with rotation policies.
- Fail-open vs fail-closed: default is fail-closed for new DEK generation; fail-over to cached DEKs for reads when allowed and policy permits (configurable per tenant).
- Minimal HSM usage: HSM root operations limited to signing and KEK unwrapping; avoid per-request HSM calls.
- Observable transitions: emit structured events whenever cached DEK is used, KEK rotation occurs, or ledger checkpoint is created.

Terraform module notes (practical):
- Provide a module: module "kms-edge" { source = "git::https://gitlab.com/redwood/modules/kms-edge.git" version = "v0.1.0" }
- Exposed variables (suggested):
  - kms_type (string) -> [vault|aws-kms|gcp-kms|pkcs11]
  - hsm_pkcs11_lib (string) -> path to PKCS#11 lib (optional)
  - keystore_path (string) -> where to store encrypted KEK metadata on disk
  - enable_dek_cache (bool)
  - dek_cache_ttl_seconds (number)
  - audit_ledger_bucket (string) -> s3-compatible endpoint or local NFS path
  - ledger_checkpoint_interval (number) -> seconds
- Important outputs:
  - wrap_key_id -> identifier of KEK (used by nodes to unwrap)
  - ledger_public_key_pem -> public key for ledger verification

Upgrade and rollout plan (staged):
1) Canary: deploy kms-edge module to 2 clusters (low-traffic) with enable_dek_cache=false and ledger writes enabled. Verify no errors and ledger entries are produced.
2) Read-cache enable: enable enable_dek_cache=true on canaries with dek_cache_ttl_seconds=300. Simulate KMS outage and validate that reads succeed for cached objects but new writes fail with clear metric.
3) HSM signing: attach HSM and enable ledger checkpoint signing (sign only). Rotate HSM credentials in a dev cluster; verify signed checkpoint verification tool works.
4) Gradually expand to all clusters; increase dek_cache_ttl_seconds as needed and monitor for stale-dek usage.

Fallback and failover semantics (detailed):
- On KMS unreachable: node attempts to use in-memory DEK cache -> if present and TTL valid, decrypt cached objects.
- If no DEK cache: if policy.allows_failover==true, node attempts to use disk-keystore (encrypted) which requires local KEK unwrap via secrets-proxy and HSM interaction; if not allowed, operation fails with clear error code KMS-UNAVAIL-FAIL_CLOSE.
- Writes that would generate new DEKs or rewrap keys are always blocked until KMS available (preventing silent downgrade).

Audit ledger design (append-only checkpoints):
- Ledger entries: JSON lines with fields: timestamp, operation, principal, object_id, dek_id, event_hash.
- Periodic checkpoint: every ledger_checkpoint_interval seconds, compute SHA256 merkle-like root over unapplied entries; submit checkpoint to HSM for signature; store signed checkpoint as checkpoint-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.sig alongside ledger file.
- Verification: independent tool (ledger-verify) accepts ledger file + checkpoint signature + public key and validates chain. Keep public key exported into terraform output (ledger_public_key_pem).
- Tamper-evidence: signed checkpoints contain previous checkpoint hash to form a chain. If a checkpoint is missing or signature mismatch, raise an alert to sec-ops channel.

Observability and SLOs to track during rollout:
- metric.kms.latency.p95 and p99 (to central KMS)
- metric.dek_cache.hits and misses
- metric.dek_cache.stale_uses (DEKs used past recommended TTL)
- metric.audit.ledger_entries_per_minute and checkpoint_sign_time
- alert.kms_unavailable_prolonged (>5m) -> escalation runbook

Test plan (essential checks):
- unit: verify envelope encryption/unwrapping flow with mock KMS and PKCS#11 simulator (SoftHSM)
- integration: simulate packet-loss / firewall rule that blackholes KMS traffic and validate cached-read behavior and alerting
- chaos: terminate the secrets-proxy on a node while workload is active; ensure fallback does not silently rewrap keys
- forensic: run ledger-verify on a day of production traffic and validate signatures and checkpoint chain

Rollback strategy:
- Keep previous terraform state around and a fast flag: enable_dek_cache -> false (global) which forces all nodes to stop using cached DEKs and require KMS for every operation.
- If HSM signing misbehaves, disable checkpoint signing and treat ledger as read-only; capture HSM logs for forensics and escalate to eng-secrets team.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- DEK TTL: what is right default? 300s is conservative but may increase KMS load; 900s reduces load but increases exposure. Need product input per customer.
- Ledger storage: S3-compatible vs local NFS. S3 improves durability and centralization but may not be allowed in air-gapped installs. For air-gapped, recommend an ops-run rotation using removable media and WORM filesystems.
- HSM vs software signing: Customers with less strict requirements might be fine with KMS-signing; we should support both modes in terraform module.

Action items (owners assigned):
- [Maya] prototype ledger-verify tool and include in infra-tools container (ETA: 2024-11-08)
- [Lucas] update terraform module variables and outputs; open MR with defaults (ETA: 2024-11-03) (gitlab MR 1214)
- [Priya] run chaos tests in canary clusters and document results (ETA: 2024-11-10)
- [Jordan] draft customer-facing one-pager explaining failover semantics and compliance implications (ETA: 2024-11-06)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a sketch. Focus feedback on the DEK TTL defaults, whether the default "fail-closed for new writes" is acceptable, and usability of the verification tool in air-gapped scenarios.

Appendix: quick terraform snippet (example usage)
module "kms_edge_instance" {
  source = "git::https://gitlab.com/redwood/modules/kms-edge.git"
  kms_type = "vault"
  enable_dek_cache = true
  dek_cache_ttl_seconds = 300
  ledger_checkpoint_interval = 600
  audit_ledger_bucket = "s3://redwood-ops-ledgers/cust-1234"
}

End of draft.
